text.text: The use of Therapeutically Applied Role-Playing Games (TA-RPGs) in mental health treatment settings has grown in popularity, with early efficacy investigations appearing promising.
However, the use of TA-RPGs for the treatment of anxiety and depression has rarely been studied in people who present with comorbid complex mental health issues.

Whilst one recent waitlist-controlled trial reported that a TA-RPG (Dungeons and Dragons with embedded CBT) reduced mental health symptomatology, this now needs to be replicated with a more robust experimental design.
Publishing this protocol methodology before the study is completed aims to increase transparency and aid other researchers conducting similar research in this advancing field.
The authors propose a two-group randomised controlled trial testing the efficacy of a CBT-infused, therapeutically applied, 8-week Dungeons and Dragons group program.
The intervention group will participate in the TA-RPG, whilst an active control group will play board games for a comparable amount of time.
Participants will consist of consumers receiving care at a community mental health centre with complex care needs and will be randomly assigned to either the intervention or active control group.

Outcome measures for anxiety and depression symptomatology will be collected before and after participation in both groups, with the intervention group also completing outcome measures at 12 months follow up.
In this protocol paper, the intervention will be outlined in detail.
A randomised controlled trial aims to add high-quality quantitative evidence of the efficacy of TA-RPG to the existing field.
Sharing this protocol ensures that the results of the study can be replicated by future researchers.

Consumers of NSW Community Mental Health (CMH) Services experience a variety of co-morbid disorders and complex healthcare needs, commonly presenting with psychotic and bipolar disorders (including schizophrenia), alongside high rates of affective, anxiety, and trauma-related symptoms (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2024).
text.formatted: Consumers of NSW Community Mental Health (CMH) Services experience a variety of co-morbid disorders and complex healthcare needs, commonly presenting with psychotic and bipolar disorders (including schizophrenia), alongside high rates of affective, anxiety, and trauma-related symptoms (Australian Institute of <ref type="bibr">Health and Welfare, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Given the diagnostic heterogeneity of community mental health populations, broadly applicable interventions are required.

Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is one of the most common conditions encountered in this setting (Achim et al., 2011; Belzer & Schneier, 2004; Pavlova et al., 2015), highlighting the need for interventions that are transdiagnostic and suitable for diverse consumers of CMH services.
text.formatted: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is one of the most common conditions encountered in this setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Achim et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Belzer & Schneier, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Pavlova et al., 2015)</ref>, highlighting the need for interventions that are transdiagnostic and suitable for diverse consumers of CMH services.

text.text: Current clinical practice guidelines recommend individual cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) as a first line treatment for adults with SAD (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2013).
CBT trials for SAD typically recruit participants with a primary diagnosis of SAD and exclude individuals with primary bipolar or psychotic disorders (Hall et al., 2025).
text.formatted: CBT trials for SAD typically recruit participants with a primary diagnosis of SAD and exclude individuals with primary bipolar or psychotic disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Hall et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the existing evidence base may have limited generalisability to adults receiving care in community mental health services, where diagnostic complexity and psychiatric comorbidity are common.

Standard CBT protocols may require significant modification when applied to individuals with complex mental health presentations, characterised by comorbidity, trauma histories, cognitive difficulties, and interpersonal challenges (Michail et al., 2017; Tarrier & Johnson, 2015).
text.formatted: Standard CBT protocols may require significant modification when applied to individuals with complex mental health presentations, characterised by comorbidity, trauma histories, cognitive difficulties, and interpersonal challenges <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Michail et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tarrier & Johnson, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, mental health clinicians have started to experiment with new approaches to delivering psychological therapies to their consumers.

One alternative approach that has increased in popularity in recent years is the use of therapeutically applied role-playing games (TA-RPGs) (Arenas et al., 2022; Hazel, 2021; Yuliawati et al., 2024).
text.formatted: One alternative approach that has increased in popularity in recent years is the use of therapeutically applied role-playing games (TA-RPGs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arenas et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Hazel, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Yuliawati et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This innovative and novel approach is offered by specialised services in the United States (e.g., Geek Therapeutics, n.d.
; The Bodhana Group, n.d.), and departs significantly from a typical CBT format.
Elements of therapy are delivered within a fantasybased role-playing game, with each participant playing the game as a character within a fictional world.
While a variety of role-playing games can be used in this context, 'Dungeons & Dragons' is the most widely recognised and therefore the most accessible.
text.formatted: While a variety of role-playing games can be used in this context, 'Dungeons & Dragons' is the most widely recognised and therefore the most accessible.

text.text: The typical format involves players sitting around a table while the game is led by a Dungeon Master, whose role is to facilitate the game, and ensure that the rules are applied fairly.

While participation in social games of Dungeons & Dragons (i.e., outside of a mental health context) has been associated with improvements in symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress (Merrick et al., 2024), as well as social connectedness (Konieczny, 2019), TA-RPG's are intentionally designed to achieve specific therapeutic objectives.
text.formatted: While participation in social games of Dungeons & Dragons (i.e., outside of a mental health context) has been associated with improvements in symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Merrick et al., 2024)</ref>, as well as social connectedness <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Konieczny, 2019)</ref>, TA-RPG's are intentionally designed to achieve specific therapeutic objectives.

text.text: In clinical TA-RPG's, mental health clinicians combine the role of Dungeon Master with that of a group facilitator, enabling them to support participants to work collaboratively and complete quests that are specifically designed to maximise the therapeutic benefits of the intervention.
Social skills are taught and practiced through interactions with non-player characters such as local merchants, the captain of the guard, and innkeepers.
Therapeutic elements are often placed within the storyline and there is ample opportunity for teachable moments within the game.
TA-RPG's have been used in therapeutic contexts to address a range of mental health and neurodevelopmental difficulties, including depression, SAD, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and substance use.

Clinical accounts have suggested that TA-RPG's may facilitate engagement in therapy among military veterans while promoting confidence, well-being, self-esteem, empathy, and frustration tolerance (Kilmer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Clinical accounts have suggested that TA-RPG's may facilitate engagement in therapy among military veterans while promoting confidence, well-being, self-esteem, empathy, and frustration tolerance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kilmer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, a recent article highlighted the growing use of role-playing games, including 'Dungeons & Dragons', by clinical psychologists in therapeutic settings across the United States, particularly with children and adolescents experiencing anxiety, depression, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), impulsivity, aggression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and ASD (Abramson, 2025).
text.formatted: Similarly, a recent article highlighted the growing use of role-playing games, including 'Dungeons & Dragons', by clinical psychologists in therapeutic settings across the United States, particularly with children and adolescents experiencing anxiety, depression, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), impulsivity, aggression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and ASD <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramson, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, these reports suggest that TA-RPGs may have useful therapeutic potential across a range of clinical populations.
However, due to the novelty of this approach, the current experimental literature demonstrating the efficacy of TA-RPG's is in its infancy.

Two recent scoping reviews have been conducted, with Yuliawati et al. (2024) highlighting the potential for TA-RPGs to promote social skills, problem-solving skills, empathy, and creativity. Arenas et al. (2022) examined table-top, computerised, live action role-play and massively multiplayer online RPGs, concluded that out of 50 studies included in the review, 90% reported positive benefits for the participants, with symptom reduction associated with several mental health conditions, including anxiety, depression, and substance use disorders, as well as supporting individuals with ASD.

(2024)</ref> highlighting the potential for TA-RPGs to promote social skills, problem-solving skills, empathy, and creativity. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Arenas et al. (2022)</ref> examined table-top, computerised, live action role-play and massively multiplayer online RPGs, concluded that out of 50 studies included in the review, 90% reported positive benefits for the participants, with symptom reduction associated with several mental health conditions, including anxiety, depression, and substance use disorders, as well as supporting individuals with ASD.

text.text: However, only 16% of the included studies used randomised controlled trials, five of which were conducted on a computerised role-playing game CBT intervention called Smart, Positive, Active, Realistic, X-factor thoughts (SPARX).
Further, these studies seldom incorporated participants presenting with complex comorbidities.

Numerous randomised controlled trials with the computerised SPARX have demonstrated improvements in mental health metrics across diverse adolescent populations, including improvements in emotional regulation and symptoms of depression and anxiety (Fleming et al., 2012; Kuosmanen et al., 2017; Merry et al., 2012; Perry et al., 2017; Poppelaars et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Numerous randomised controlled trials with the computerised SPARX have demonstrated improvements in mental health metrics across diverse adolescent populations, including improvements in emotional regulation and symptoms of depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Fleming et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Kuosmanen et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Merry et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Perry et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Poppelaars et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Although SPARX currently offers the strongest evidence supporting the effectiveness of a gamified CBT intervention, its computerised design differs notably from that of TA-RPG's.
TA-RPGs are typically delivered in group settings and are facilitated by a mental health professional, offering a more interactive and social experience.

Despite growing interest in this format, high-quality experimental research on the efficacy of TA-RPGs remains limited and it is not clear whether, and under what conditions, TA-RPGs produce meaningful clinical benefits.
To our knowledge few studies have investigated the effectiveness of TA-RPG's for individuals with complex mental health conditions accessing community mental health services.
A recent waitlist-controlled trial explored the use of TA-RPG's in an adult community mental health setting in Sydney, Australia (Rae et al., 2025).

text.text: The transdiagnostic sample included 33 participants that were aged 18-65, and the most common primary mental health diagnoses included schizophrenia, first-episode psychosis and bipolar disorder.
The role-playing game was 'CBT-infused', meaning that the CBT concepts were embedded throughout an existing role-playing game framework.
This was designed to occur as organically as possible within the game, while maintaining player immersion.

The study reported that relative to a waitlist control group receiving treatment as usual, the TA-RPG significantly reduced participants self-reported symptoms of social anxiety, depression, and self-esteem.
Whilst these results are encouraging; the study was limited by the small sample size and quasi-randomisation to the waitlist control vs. experimental group.
The current protocol details a randomised controlled trial (RCT) using the same intervention, with an active control group that play commercially-available board games.

Analogous to Rae et al. (2025), the present RCT focuses on the presence and severity of clinically-relevant symptoms rather than categorical diagnoses, with outcome measures selected to reflect the intervention's therapeutic targets and mechanisms.

text.text: Finally, board games were chosen as an active control group to control for non-specific effects of group participation, social interaction, enjoyment, and engagement, while differing from the TA-RPG in the specific therapeutic mechanisms hypothesised to drive change.
This design therefore allowed the effects of the TA-RPG intervention to be distinguished from the broader benefits of participating in a structured, enjoyable group activity.
The hypotheses and analysis plans were preregistered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry [link redacted for peer review].

It is hypothesised that an 8week, CBT-infused TA-RPG group program will (1) show a significant difference in the reduction of self-reported social anxiety symptoms as compared to a board game control group, (2) show improvements in self-reported symptoms of depression, self-esteem, and PTSD, and (3) these improvements will be maintained at a follow-up 12 months after completion of the group.
A secondary aim of the study is to further test the effectiveness of running TA-RPG groups within the current structure of the services that are provided in a public mental health system.
A CBT-infused TA-RPG is not intended to replace a structured CBT program, as it does not provide the same level of structure, organisation, and predictability as a traditional CBT intervention.

However, given the limitations of delivering structured CBT to people with complex mental health presentations, the results of the current study hopes to demonstrate evidence for the effectiveness of a creative alternative for consumers of community mental health services.

It is anticipated that the results of this study will add to the growing literature base for the use of TA-RPGs in clinical practice, and improve the likelihood of public mental health services adopting therapies that reflect their diverse consumers.

text.text: The inclusion criteria are as follows: (1) have an open encounter (NSW Health term for the mental health team responsible for the consumer's clinical governance) with an eligible community mental health service within Sydney Local Health District (SLHD), (2) be 16 to 65 years old (this accounts for all consumers in a typical adult CMH service, as well as the older portion of adolescent services) (3) have an interest in attending the group, (4) be fluent in English, (5) refrain from being under the influence of alcohol or substances while attending the group sessions (6) be willing to interact respectively with other participants (7) be available to attend group sessions for 8 consecutive weeks, and (8) be able to use a smart device or computer with wi-fi/internet connection.

Exclusion criteria are as follows: (1) severe cognitive impairment, (2) in an acute phase of a severe mental illness that would preclude the person from participating, and (3) deemed to be a high risk to self or others by the individual's treating team.

Due to resourcing constraints, no structured clinical interview will be conducted, and current diagnostic status will therefore not be used as an inclusion or exclusion criterion, consistent with the aim of providing an inclusive intervention accessible to consumers of community mental health services irrespective of diagnosis.

A two-group randomised controlled trial (RCT) will be conducted with participants randomly allocated to either the Dungeons and Dragons Intervention group or the active control group that will play standard, commercially available board games for the same amount of time.

We selected an 8-week intervention period to provide sufficient time for participants to engage with and practise the CBT-based skills incorporated into the TA-RPG, while maintaining a feasible intervention duration.
Participants in the active control group will be invited to complete the Dungeons and Dragons Intervention group following their completion of the board-game control group.
This is to ensure that all participants have fair and equitable access to the TA-RPG intervention.

Recruitment will be completed via advertising to care coordinators, stakeholders and mental health treating teams through in-service presentations, emails, attendance at meetings, and brochure circulation.
Participants are encouraged to contact the Primary Investigator (PI) with any questions regarding the study.
After a brief screening process, participants will be asked to provide informed consent before continuing in the study.
Care coordinators will contact the PI directly to discuss the suitability of a referral to the study.
The PI will ask questions based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria.
If the PI is contacted by a stakeholder or member of a treating team who is not the care coordinator, the PI will contact the care coordinator to discuss the referral.
Demographic information will be collected from the consumer's Electronic Medical Record (EMR).
This information includes consumer's age, gender, Medical Record Number (MRN), current phone number, and medication regime.
The PI will record the participants diagnosis based on the information found in their Electronic Medical Record to ensure accuracy.
Once a participant has been deemed appropriate for the study, the PI will contact the participant and arrange a one-on-one interview.
Participants will be asked to provide an email address so that they can be sent material relating to character choices in preparation for the one-on-one interview.

During the one-on-one interview, the PI will discuss the study at length to ensure the individual understands the requirements of the study and provide ample opportunities for the participant to ask questions before making the decision to provide informed consent.

Once consent has been provided, the participants will create a character to be used in the Dungeons and Dragons intervention and be informed of the expected start times and dates for their participation in the study.
All participants, regardless of group allocation, will create a character during the one-on-one interview.
The LSAS has 24 items that measure the level of fear and avoidance of social situations that is typical of people who experience social anxiety.
On a 4-point Likert scale, participants how fearful they are, and to what extent they would avoid, a variety of social situations.
Examples include telephoning in public, meeting strangers, and going to a party.
The LSAS-SR has good internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity (Fresco et al., 2001; Rytwinski et al., 2009), and is sensitive to treatment change (Baker et al., 2002).

text.text: The 21 items in the BDI-II measure the severity of symptoms that are indicative of depression including pessimism, worthlessness, sadness, and irritability.

A comprehensive review of the psychometric properties of the BDI-II across 118 studies concluded that the measure demonstrates high internal consistency, good test-retest reliability, strong validity, and an excellent ability to discriminate between depressed and non-depressed individuals (Wang & Gorenstein, 2013).

text.text: The PTSD checklist measures the frequency and severity of symptoms relating to PTSD.
The scale includes 17 items that require participants to rate the extent to which they are bothered by trauma-related issues and problems in the last month, ranging from "not at all" to "extremely."
These problems include hypervigilance, emotional numbness, intrusive thoughts, nightmares or images, difficulty sleeping, and angry outbursts.

Participants will be asked to complete all outcome measures one week prior to their participation in either the intervention (DnD) or control (board game) groups.
Group schedules will be determined by several factors including participant availability, PI and secondary facilitator availability, room availability and recruitment.
Post outcome measures will be completed in the final session (week 8) for each group.
Participants in the intervention group will also complete the outcome measures at 12 months post-completion of the group.

Risk assessments will be completed on an ongoing basis throughout the trial.
This will include assessment of risk of harm to self or others.
The PI is a Clinical Psychologist and the primary facilitator for every intervention and control group.
The primary and secondary facilitators are trained in risk management.
If a participant is deemed to be at a higher risk compared to baseline, the PI has the option of withdrawing the participant from the study.
The presence of an increased risk will not automatically exclude the participant from the study, however, increased assessment and monitoring of their mental state will be conducted.
The PI will communicate the risk to the relevant participant's care coordinator as soon as practicable, and in the event of an immediate risk, local safety protocols will be followed.
This may include accessing emergency services.

If a participant is identified as being at immediate risk during a session, the co-facilitator will provide immediate support and facilitate access to appropriate crisis intervention or emergency services, as required, while the primary facilitator continues to deliver the group session.
To support participant safety throughout the intervention, "Resting at the Inn" cards are incorporated into each session.
These cards provide participants with an opportunity to temporarily withdraw from gameplay and access support if they experience distress or feel overwhelmed.
During this period, the participant's character remains inactive and does not lose progress, with the character considered to be safely resting at the nearest inn.
Further details regarding the use and implementation of the "Resting at the Inn" cards are provided at section Intervention Manual (below).
Each group program is one continuous story that takes place over 8 weeks using the 5 th Edition of Dungeons and Dragons (Crawford et al., 2014).

text.text: Dungeons and Dragons is owned by 'Wizards of the Coast' and represents a system of rules and mechanics that allow a game to be played (without providing the content of a game).
There are two main options for playing Dungeons and Dragons, the first is to purchase a commercially available published campaign and the second is to create an original or "home brew" game.
The intervention used in this study represents the latter, using an original storyline with some concepts and themes that have been drawn from popular culture and science fiction.

The primary facilitator (Dungeon Master) is responsible for setting the scene, role-playing the non-player characters that will interact with the participant's characters, and provide the rules and structure of the game.
The secondary facilitator assists the Dungeon Master with monitoring and managing the group dynamics as well as assisting the participants within the game.
The secondary facilitator plays the game alongside the participants, using their own character.
From this vantage point, they can assist the participants with the challenges that they are facing, in a subtle way that won't break the immersion.
One example would be if the participants are asked what they would like to do in a given situation and are undecided.
The secondary facilitator will be able to use their character to make suggestions of things that might be helpful.

The intervention's original storyline was developed through a series of brainstorming sessions involving mental health clinicians, peer workers, and individuals with lived experience of mental health challenges.
The story begins with a call for aid from the Kingdom of Waterkeep, which faces a dire threat.
An evil sorcerer has unleashed a magical plague upon one of its cities-a curse that manifests with symptoms mirroring that of depression.
To save the kingdom, a group of adventurers is enlisted to locate four enchanted crystals.
Each crystal represents a mental health theme; trauma, anxiety, depression, and social isolation or exclusion, and the participants battle a monster that corresponds to that theme.
For example, a wraith represents depression, and uses powers such as motivation drain, hopelessness, slowed motor functions, and a cognitive fog.
By defeating each monster and answering psychoeducation questions, the players can activate each crystal.
Only by activating and uniting all four crystals can the curse be broken and the evil sorcerer defeated in a final showdown.
Throughout the campaign, adventurers will encounter a variety of non-player characters (NPCs) designed with distinct personality traits and communication styles.
These include traits such as perfectionism, optimism, arrogance, low emotional intelligence, friendliness, and abruptness.
These personalities were intentionally selected to represent diverse interpersonal interaction styles, thereby providing opportunities for participants to practise social communication skills.
The perfectionist character was additionally designed to facilitate self-reflection on participants' own perfectionistic traits, where relevant.
Each group will consist of up to six participants, a primary facilitator, and a cofacilitator.
Groups will commence once a minimum of four participants have enrolled.
The two-hour sessions will be delivered primarily in person, with occasional online attendance available for participants who are unable to attend face-to-face.
Groups will typically be conducted once per week, with multiple groups scheduled consecutively rather than running simultaneously.
Once a group has commenced, it will continue through to completion provided at least one participant remains enrolled.
If participant attrition results in a group falling below four participants after commencement, the group will continue where feasible rather than being discontinued.
The therapeutically applied Dungeons & Dragons program used in this study was intentionally designed to incorporate elements of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT).

text.text: A generic, transdiagnostic CBT protocol was developed to reflect the complex presentations of participants in community mental health services.
The intervention incorporates evidencebased CBT strategies from multiple protocols, with the strongest emphasis on social anxiety.

These strategies include psychoeducation, repeated in-session exposure to social interactions, and the identification and restructuring of unhelpful cognitions (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, 2013).
Social skills training, problem solving, and collaborative teamwork are also present throughout the intervention.
This approach provides facilitators with the flexibility to address diverse clinical needs while maintaining a coherent therapeutic framework.
The intervention manual can be accessed on the Open Science Framework (Rae & Jennings, 2026).

text.text: Given the flexible and dynamic nature of role-playing games, there is no fixed sequence in which CBT skills are practiced during the 8-week program.
However, all key skills are introduced to participants at various points throughout the sessions, often reinforced multiple times.
Previous evaluation of the intervention demonstrated reductions in social anxiety symptoms irrespective of the order in which the therapeutic skills were introduced (Rae et al., 2025).

text.text: Due to the interactive nature of role-playing games, each intervention varies according to participants' decisions and gameplay.

However, all groups are required to complete the core therapeutic content, which includes four mandatory modules addressing (1) depression, (2) trauma, (3) anxiety, and (4) social inclusion and identity concerns.
In addition, all groups participate in structured social encounters and a final encounter with the primary antagonist.

The treatment manual also includes a series of optional encounters, which the group facilitator may incorporate at their discretion based on participant engagement, group progress, and available session time.
Where appropriate, the Dungeon Master integrates participants' character backstories into optional side quests to enhance engagement and personalise the therapeutic experience.

Participants in the board game control group will be asked to meet at a regular weekly time over the course of 8 weeks, for 2 hours in duration.
This will mimic the structure of the Dungeons and Dragons intervention group.
The sessions will be run by the PI, with the help of a co-facilitator.
During the first session, expectations will be discussed including group safety and boundaries.
For example, participants are informed about what to expect from the group, including the procedures that will be followed if a participant becomes distressed.
They are also invited to identify factors that would help create a safe and supportive environment conducive to full participation.
The role of the facilitators is to ensure the safety of the participants, while encouraging the use of the board games.
The participants will be provided with a variety of commercially available, non-role play games to play for the duration of each session.
The participants will be encouraged to choose the games they would like to play.
The only stipulation that was placed on the choice of board games was that they can't be a role-playing game.

Board games offered to participants in the board game group include: Sequence, Citadels, Carcassonne, Cranium, Pictionary, Ticket to Ride, Scrabble, Jenga, Uno, Operation, Jumanji, Tsuro, Code Names, No thanks, Battleship, Monopoly, Scattergories, Sushi Go, Taboo, Articulate.
All data collected will be stored securely and de-identified to ensure confidentiality.
A linear mixed-model analysis will be used to examine significant changes in anxiety scores over time as a function of intervention/control group assignment.
Individual participants (first level analysis) will be nested in weekly participation groups (second level analysis).
Variables at the first level will include age, gender, time (pre vs.post), intervention group (intervention vs. control) and the interaction between time and intervention group.
The nesting of participants within specific weekly participation groups will be specified through a random effect for the participant group-level structure (Level 2).
Where a significant interaction is found, the magnitude of change (pre vs. post) will be compared between groups and contextualised with reference to minimal important difference.
Sensitivity analyses will be conducted to help identify and determine the effect of potential confounders (such as primary mental health diagnosis or medication use).
Analyses will be repeated to examine the effects of intervention/control group assignment on depression scores, PTSD symptoms and selfesteem over time.
Participants that complete at least five out of eight sessions and complete both pre and post outcome measures will be included in the data analysis.

A minimum attendance threshold of five of the eight sessions was established, as participants missing three or more sessions would not receive over one-third of the intervention content, potentially reducing treatment effectiveness.
Missing data will not be imputed.
Reasons for drop out will be documented (where possible), to inform future interventions.
Participants who drop out after randomisation but before the intervention begins, will be counted separately to those who drop out after the intervention begins.
Drop-out rates (proportion) will be compared between groups using Chi Squared test.
Results of the post group evaluation questionnaire will be examined to identify trends in responses.
This will provide important contextual information that can help in interpret the results and may inform future versions of the intervention program.

A paired-samples t-test will be used to compare the immediate post-intervention outcome measures to the 12-month follow-up to determine whether improvements made in the intervention group are maintained 12 months after its completion.
Bayesian t-tests will be used to quantify the strength of evidence for the null vs. alternative hypothesis.

text.text: TA-RPG's are increasing in popularity as a potential treatment for symptoms of depression and anxiety in mental health settings.

A recent study identified that a CBTinfused, TA-RPG can reduce self-report symptoms of social anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem in a sample of adult consumers in community mental health services in Sydney Australia (Rae et al., 2025).

text.text: The primary aim of the current study is to replicate the findings using a more robust experimental design, including random group assignment and a larger sample size.
It is anticipated that this study will contribute to the current evidence base of TA-RPG's for adults with complex mental health issues.

It is hoped that by publishing this protocol, providing a transparent methodology, and the details of our TA-RPG intervention, other researchers in this field will be able to replicate our study design, advance it, or provide criticism in good faith.

table.html: Element of Therapy Method of Delivery Self-esteem, acceptance of others and leadership Reinforced throughout all sessions via skills gameplay, character interactions, and facilitator reflection. Managing perfectionism Embedded within narrative encounters and post-session discussion. SUDS scales and practice rating levels of distress Introduced in Session 1 and rated at the start and completion of each session. Kindness, compassion and empathy Reinforced through narrative encounters, role-play, and group reflection. Overcoming peer pressure Practised through specific narrative encounters requiring decision-making. Acceptance of failure/poor performance, Reinforced throughout gameplay and challenging situations facilitator feedback. Social skills training including effective communication, assertiveness and understanding others.
